source_read: PMC HTML, PMC4748442: abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Tables 1-3 (HTML tables), Figure 1-3 legends, Discussion, funding/disclosure and acknowledgments read in full. Figures not inspected as images. Supplementary Tables 1-2 (.doc downloads) not opened.

claims.overstatement: Wording is careful. One nuance not in the claim: the 17 who stayed abstinent were the less elevated users at scan 1 (full striatum 2.85 vs 3.38 in the 7 who relapsed), the within-person drop was not significant (-11%, p=0.055; range -34% to +29%, 6 of 17 rose), and only 9 controls were rescanned, so 'did not differ' at scan 2 is an imprecise non-difference (editors' g 0.21, 95% CI -0.60 to 1.02), not shown equivalence.
claims.note: Supported from this source: 2.6 days, 28 vs 22, +28%, BPND 3.09 (0.71) vs 2.41 (0.34), p<0.0001; correlations with frequency, cumulative dose, days since use and plasma level; scan-2 values 2.54 (0.39) in 17 vs 2.46 (0.34) in 9, not different; the authors' interpretation (less competition from depleted vesicular dopamine) and their admission that it is not directly tested. Not reproduced: the editors' g. With pooled SD and Hedges' correction I get g = 1.16 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.76) (Cohen's d 1.18; d with the unweighted average of the two variances 1.22), not 1.24 (0.63 to 1.85). Not in this source: 'post-mortem VMAT2 reported normal' (Boileau 2016 says only that human findings are equivocal) and the '~10% lower' figure for the long-abstinence PET study (Boileau 2016 cites Johanson 2006 as an example of decreased binding after longer abstinence, without a number). Minor: scan-2 abstinence is 9.9 (SD 2.3) days in Table 2 but 'mean 9.8' in the Table 3 footnote.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Results > MA users have greater (+)[11C]DTBZ binding during early abstinence; Table 3 (first scan, full striatum)
anchors.extracted: Scan 1 at mean 2.6 days (range 1-7) after last use: full-striatum BPND 3.09 +/- 0.71 in 28 methamphetamine users vs 2.41 +/- 0.34 in 22 controls, +28%, p<0.0001 (Bonferroni-corrected); regional +31% associative, +24% limbic, +26% sensorimotor; cocaine users (n=9) 2.55 +/- 0.30, +6%, p=1.0. Group main effect F(2,56)=9.581. Effect held after adjustment for cigarettes per day, alcohol, cannabis and depressive symptoms (F 5.0-5.7, p 0.006-0.011).
Days abstinent before scan 1: 2.6 +/- 2.0 (n=28); before scan 2: 9.9 +/- 2.3 (n=17); Table 3 legend gives scan 2 as 7-15 days, mean 9.8.

anchors.locator: Results > Higher (+)[11C]DTBZ binding in MA users during early abstinence correlated with severity of recent drug use..., para 1
anchors.extracted: In the 28 users at scan 1, full-striatum binding correlated with frequency of recent use (r=0.68, p<0.0001), last-month cumulative dose (r=0.48, p=0.009) and plasma methamphetamine (r=0.5, p=0.008); days of abstinence correlated negatively in associative striatum (r=-0.49, p=0.008). Those who had used ~24 h before (n=10) had higher binding than those 2-7 days out (n=18). Correlations uncorrected for multiple testing.

anchors.locator: Results > Rapid recovery of (+)[11C]DTBZ binding in some MA users; Table 3 (second scan)
anchors.extracted: Rescanned ~1 week later (about 10 days since last use): 17 users who stayed abstinent 2.54 +/- 0.39 vs 9 controls 2.46 +/- 0.34 (+3%), cocaine users (n=8) +5%, F(2,48)=0.288, p=0.751. Within users, mean change from scan 1 -11% (p=0.055), range -34% to +29%; 6/17 increased. 7 users relapsed and were not rescanned; 4 more not rescanned for other reasons. Abstainers' scan-1 full striatum 2.85 +/- 0.74 vs relapsers 3.38 +/- 0.59 (relapsers 17% higher, ANCOVA p=0.035). Scan-1 binding predicted scan-2 binding (full striatum r=0.54).

Authors interpret elevated binding as depleted vesicular dopamine (less competition with the tracer at VMAT2), but state they cannot exclude a compensatory change in VMAT2 protein or reduced binding from residual methamphetamine at scan 1; later they say it remains to be established whether low stored dopamine means low synaptic dopamine. No direct dopamine measure was made in vivo.

Human VMAT2 findings in methamphetamine users called equivocal (citing Johanson 2006, Kitamura 2007, Tong 2014, Wilson 1996a); longer abstinence might reveal decreased binding, e.g., Johanson 2006. No percentage given and no statement that post-mortem VMAT2 was normal.

claims.note: The source supports the claim's framing: the authors state that their users' VMAT2 binding was not decreased as it is in known dopamine-neuron loss, that this could be masking by dopamine depletion, but that it is 'perhaps more likely' that use at these levels did not cause toxic loss of vesicles or neurons; they also warn that DTBZ binding (a standard terminal-integrity marker) is confounded by dopamine levels.

anchors.extracted: Animal data show high-dose methamphetamine can damage dopamine neurons and lower VMAT2, but human findings are equivocal; binding was not decreased in this sample; possible masking by acute dopamine-lowering, or, which the authors consider perhaps more likely, no toxic loss of vesicles or neurons at the amounts these participants used (mean 0.35 g/day by self-report).
Findings 'raise additional caution' in reading DTBZ differences as reflecting only VMAT2 protein change, i.e., the terminal marker is sensitive to vesicular dopamine content.

key_findings.correction: Values are as printed, but the printed p-values do not match the printed statistics: F(2,56)=9.581 gives p=0.0003 (printed <0.0001); F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077 gives p=0.015 (printed 0.001, which matches the uncorrected df F(4,112)). Conclusions unchanged; suggest adding as a reporting issue.

Editors' g not reproduced. Hedges' g with pooled SD (n-1 weights) and small-sample correction J=1-3/(4N-9), n=28 vs 22, from Table 3: whole striatum 1.16 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.76); associative 1.28 (0.67 to 1.89); sensorimotor 1.10 (0.50 to 1.70); limbic 0.83 (0.25 to 1.41). Cohen's d whole striatum 1.18; d with the unweighted mean of the two variances 1.22 (assoc 1.35, sensorimotor 1.16, limbic 0.88). None of the standard variants gives 1.24 (0.63 to 1.85) for whole striatum. The claim cl_meth_vmat2 magnitude ('editors' g about 1.24, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.85') should read about 1.16 (0.56 to 1.76).
As printed. Note the paper lists four covariates but gives three F results 'respectively', so which model each F belongs to is ambiguous.
Mean 9.9 days is from Table 2; the Table 3 legend gives mean 9.8 (range 7-15).

The days-abstinent correlation (r=-0.49, p=0.008) is for associative striatum only; frequency (r=0.68), past-month amount (r=0.48) and plasma level (r=0.5) are whole striatum. The '45-52% above controls' for the ~24 h group is 52/45/45% in associative/limbic/sensorimotor striatum.

The VMAT2-protein and residual-methamphetamine caveats are in Discussion paragraph 5 (correct); the statement that it remains to be established whether low stored dopamine means low synaptic dopamine is in Discussion paragraph 7 ('Does low brain dopamine have any therapeutic relevance?'), not paragraph 9 (the 9-paragraph Discussion ends with the summary paragraph).

reporting_issues.note: With 34 rescanned participants in 3 groups the error df would be 31; 48 implies 51.

0.35 g/day x ~17-18 use days per month (49.9/90 days; 4.3 days/week) is roughly 6 g, against 1.57 g/month printed. Means of products need not equal products of means, but a fourfold gap is not explained by that.

Recomputed for n=28 (two-tailed): r=0.46 gives p=0.014; r=0.43 gives p=0.022 (printed 0.03); r=0.44 gives p=0.019 (printed 0.011); r=0.37 gives p=0.053 (printed 0.051, consistent); r=0.48, 0.49, 0.5 consistent.

Repeated F=5.723 and unexplained df 43 confirmed. But the paper lists four covariates (cigarettes, alcohol, cannabis, depressive symptoms) and three results 'respectively', so attributing the first F to 'the cigarettes model' and the third to a 'cannabis-plus-depression model' is the card's inference, not stated in the paper. The p-values (0.006, 0.011, 0.006) match their printed F and df.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall agreed. The judgment fits the recovery and cognition conclusions; for the scan-1 difference used by cl_meth_vmat2 the bias concern is mostly confounding (education, IQ, smoking, cocaine co-exposure in 17/28 by hair), and the size and recency-dependence of the difference make confounding an unlikely full explanation, which the card's reasoning already says.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' agreed. One addition: the abstract says binding correlated with withdrawal symptoms, but the withdrawal questionnaire correlation was r=0.37, p=0.051; only daytime sleepiness (r=0.44) reached p<0.05.

missed: Printed p-values for the main ANOVA do not match the printed statistics: group F(2,56)=9.581 gives p=0.0003 (printed p<0.0001); ROI x group F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077 gives p=0.015 (printed p=0.001, which matches uncorrected df 4,112). Results > MA users have greater (+)[11C]DTBZ binding, para 1.

Precision of the 'did not differ' finding at scan 2: editors' g for 17 abstainers vs 9 controls, whole striatum, is 0.21 (95% CI -0.60 to 1.02) from Table 3, so a moderate-to-large residual elevation is not excluded. Relevant to the wording of cl_meth_vmat2.
Abstract reports a correlation with withdrawal symptoms; the Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire correlation was r=0.37, p=0.051 (Results, correlations paragraph 2).

Discussion para 5 calls the regional imaging differences 'only slight (and not statistically significant)' while quoting AST +31% and SMST +26%, both p<0.0001 vs controls in the Results; the sentence presumably means the between-subregion difference, but as written it contradicts Table 3.

Discussion para 6: the authors say it is 'perhaps more likely' that the amounts these participants used did not cause toxic loss of dopamine vesicles or neurons. This is the anchor for cl_meth_dopamine_damage and is not among the card's key findings.

Discussion para 6 describes human VMAT2 findings as equivocal and does not say post-mortem VMAT2 was normal or give a ~10% figure; the card does not record this, but cl_meth_vmat2 should not rest those two statements on this source.
